Share SOC2 + KMS whitepaper and network diagram (Priya)
Provision trial sandbox with two routes and sample workload (Catalyst to confirm config)
Follow up with pricing/committed capacity options and pilot SOW

Priya - export latency + cost baseline for customer's avg payload by 2026-12-04

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Mark Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jake Morris (Catalyst Labs, CTO), Lina Gomez (Catalyst DevOps), Sasha Patel (Head of ML)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial):
- Walkthrough of Redwood Console per-route usage dashboards, cost breakdown and attribution.
- Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for Catalyst's regulated workflows.
- Security checklist (SOC2, KMS, SSO) requested.
- Agreement to spin up a 1-week pilot sandbox with two production-like routes and sample traffic.

Topics covered:
- Per-route attribution and cost heatmaps
- Prefix/KV cache impact on token-costs
- Batching windows and latency tradeoffs
- Rollout strategies and fallbacks (canary/A-B/fallback to smaller models)
- Security/SSO/KMS and audit logging

Transcript body:
[00:00] Mark Reed: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Jake, Lina, Sasha, we really appreciate it. I'm Mark, AE on the Redwood Console team. Priya's gonna take the demo and show our per-route dashboards.
[00:18] Jake Morris: Hey, Mark. Thanks. We're excited, we've been looking at ways to get more visibility into inference costs across our product areas.
[00:25] Priya Nair: Great, I'll share my screen in a sec. Quick agenda: console tour -> per-route and route-lens -> cost breakdown -> security and deployment options -> Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:34] Lina Gomez: Yep, sounds good. We're particularly interested in measuring route-level spend and pinning model versions for compliance.
[00:42] Sasha Patel: Also curious about prefix caching and how it affects token counts for our chat histories.
[00:46] Priya Nair: Perfect, we'll cover that. (screen share starts) So this is the Redwood Console. Top nav is usage, models, routes, billing, and optimize. I'll jump into Routes first — here's Catalyst-Labs default workspace we set up for the demo.
[01:10] Priya Nair: You can see a route list, each route maps to an API route or microservice. For the demo I created two: "assist-search" and "support-chat-prod" to mimic what you described in the intake.
[01:25] Jake Morris: Nice, the names line up with our internal service names which will make mapping easier.
[01:32] Priya Nair: If I click into support-chat-prod you'll see a summary at the top: request rate, p50/p95 latency, token consumption, and cost per 1k requests. We also show a live trace sampling.
[01:44] Mark Reed: Quick note: the cost numbers are derived from our per-token billing model but adjusted with batching and cache savings applied. So you'll see raw token cost and effective billed cost after batching/caching offsets.
[01:58] Lina Gomez: How do you attribute cache savings? Sometimes the KV cache reduces token output dramatically and we need to account for that in finance.
[02:07] Priya Nair: Good question. We show a 'cache delta' line in the cost breakdown; it's estimated from prefix hits and KV hit rates. The delta is broken down by model variant, so you can see which quantized or fp16 variant benefited most.
[02:22] Sasha Patel: Are the cache hits deterministic across versions? If we change model versions, how stable is the hit rate?
[02:29] Priya Nair: It depends — when we swap model families, prefix match semantics can shift a bit. We recommend pinning model versions per-route for a canary, and the console has a 'compare' view to look at hit rate pre/post rollout.
[02:41] Jake Morris: Show us the compare view.
[02:44] Priya Nair: Sure. (navigates) Compare lets you overlay two time windows and two model versions. Here you can see that when we moved support-chat-prod from a 8-bit quantized variant to the fp16 variant the latency p95 improved but token output increased by ~7%, which changed the cost per request.
[03:05] Mark Reed: That's a typical tradeoff — latency vs cost. Redwood Optimize gives model/quantization recommendations based on your SLO and cost target, but the console shows the raw numbers so finance can reconcile.
[03:18] Lina Gomez: For dedicated or private deployments, do these cost numbers still reflect actual on-prem consumption or are they just estimates?
[03:26] Priya Nair: If you're on Dedicated, we can plug actual reserved capacity utilization and hourly GPU math into the dashboard so you'll see true unit economics. For Private on-prem we ingest your capacity config and give you a per-token equivalent cost based on your hardware profile. There's usually some alignment work during onboarding.
[03:42] Jake Morris: Okay, that's helpful. One of our requirements is retention of audit logs for 2 years — does Redwood Console surface those?
[03:49] Priya Nair: Yes, audit logs are exportable. For Private deployments you control retention via your storage, and for Hosted we have an add-on retention package. I'll flag Priya — (laugh) sorry, Mark: Priya will share the SOC2/retention doc after the call.
[04:00] Mark Reed: (chuckles) Yeah, we'll drop the whitepaper.
[04:04] Sasha Patel: On the per-route cost breakdown, can we get a CSV export for cost allocation to chargeback different product teams?
[04:11] Priya Nair: Absolutely, there's a 'Download cost report' button and you can scoping by tag, route, model, and time window. It's meant to plug into your internal FinOps.
[04:20] Lina Gomez: Are there RBAC controls to prevent devs from changing model pins without approvals? We need approvals for production changes.
[04:28] Priya Nair: Yes, RBAC with SSO/SAML is supported. You can create roles that are read-only for finance, deploy-only for ops, and admin for platform. All actions are audit-logged.
[04:36] Jake Morris: Good. Let's dig into the cost model details — show us how batching parameters appear in the console.
[04:43] Priya Nair: Sure, under the Route -> Performance section we show batching windows, target latency and observed throughput. You can adjust the batching policy; we expose knobs for max batch size, max wait ms, and a cost estimator that simulates effective tokens saved when batching is enabled.
[04:58] Mark Reed: And note, continuous batching helps maximize GPU utilization so the effective per-token cost drops, but if your SLO is strict you might limit batch windows and lose some savings. The console will show the modeled tradeoff.
[05:11] Sasha Patel: Any chance to run a simulated workload to see the modeled impact before we change prod settings?
[05:16] Priya Nair: Yep, that's one of the Optimize features — run a 'what-if' simulation using your sample traces. We can ingest a week of traces and show alternate batch configs and quantization combos.
[05:27] Jake Morris: Could you show an example simulation?
[05:30] Priya Nair: (switches) Here's a sample trace we loaded. If I toggle quantize to int8 (8-bit) and increase batch window from 10ms to 40ms, the simulator predicts a 32% reduction in billed token cost with a median latency increase of ~12ms.
[05:46] Lina Gomez: 12ms is acceptable for search but support-chat needs sub-120ms p95 — what's the impact there?
[05:52] Priya Nair: For p95-sensitive routes you can set hard SLOs at the route level; the optimizer will only recommend configs that meet the SLO. In this case the sim flagged that int8 + 40ms batch exceeded the p95 target, so it proposed a mixed config: int8 for background inference and fp16 for real-time, plus prefix caching.
[06:13] Mark Reed: We also have rollout templates so you can canary the new config on 10% of traffic and monitor your quality metrics. If quality drops we automatically rollback to the previous config.
[06:24] Jake Morris: Speaking of quality, do you have quant metrics for hallucinations or eval hooks? We run unit prompt sets to validate quality after changes.
[06:33] Priya Nair: We integrate your eval sets. The console can run canary evals as part of the rollout and show metric deltas — Rouge-like score, specificity, hallucination rate (heuristic), and user-facing error rates.
[06:46] Sasha Patel: Can the console tie an eval regression directly to cost changes? For example, we don't want to hide quality regressions that happen only when using cheaper quantized variants.
[06:55] Priya Nair: Yes — the waveform compares model variants and flags regressions that coincide with changes in cost-per-request, so you get correlated view: cost + quality.
[07:05] Lina Gomez: Let's talk deployment modes: we may try Hosted for a pilot but ultimately need Private VPC due to data residency. What are the main gaps when moving from Hosted to Private?
[07:16] Mark Reed: The console experience is the same across modes. The main differences are network topology and control plane location. For Private you run a customer-managed control plane, we provide an operator package. For Hosted, Redwood's control plane manages routing. Data plane behavior — caching and prefix handling — is the same, but for Private we defer to your KMS and audit pipeline.
[07:38] Jake Morris: Any differences in observability retention or sampling? We need raw token traces for 90 days.
[07:45] Priya Nair: On Hosted, the observability retention is configurable with an add-on. On Private, you can send telemetry to your metrics/ELK stack; we provide exporters and the console can still surface an aggregated view.
[07:57] Sasha Patel: You mentioned fallback policies earlier. If our primary model is unavailable, can the route fall back to a smaller model automatically?
[08:04] Priya Nair: Yes, smart routing policies allow you to specify fallback sequences: e.g., model A (fp16, p95 80ms) -> model B (int8 smaller) -> model C (cpu-based NLL proxy). You can also fallback by region or capacity tier.
[08:18] Jake Morris: Can we set cost caps per route to avoid runaway spend?
[08:22] Priya Nair: There are per-route budget alerts and soft caps. The system can throttle or reject requests if a hard cap is reached, but most customers prefer alerts and automated fallbacks to cheaper variants to preserve availability.
[08:36] Lina Gomez: Show us the alerts UI.
[08:39] Priya Nair: (scrolls) Alerts are under Ops -> Alerts. You can create threshold alerts for token spend, spend rate, latency SLO breaches, and model-specific error rates. Alerts can post to Slack, PagerDuty, or webhooks.
[08:52] Mark Reed: For billing alignment we also surface per-token chargebacks daily and provide tags for cost centers.
[08:59] Jake Morris: How granular can tags be? Can we tag by user-facing product, feature flag, or request metadata?
[09:06] Priya Nair: Tagging is flexible. You can pass metadata in the request header and Redwood will surface it as labels for routing, attribution, and filtering in the console. We also have automatic service name mapping for common frameworks.
[09:18] Sasha Patel: We heard about KV cache prefixing earlier. Can you demo how a long chat history affects tokenization and cost?
[09:24] Priya Nair: Sure. Here's a support-chat-prod trace with a 5-turn conversation. With no prefix cache the generation token count is 420 tokens; with prefix/KV cache enabled the generation is 110 tokens because the prompt context is cached. The console shows the hit rate and the estimated savings line item in the cost waterfall.
[09:44] Lina Gomez: Does the console show which specific prompts are cache hits so we can tune templates?
[09:49] Priya Nair: We anonymize content by default but surface pattern buckets like 'greeting sequence' or 'order-status retrieval' so you can tune templates without exposing PII.
[09:59] Jake Morris: On security: for Private we need HSM-backed KMS for key wraps. Does Redwood support HSM integration?
[10:06] Priya Nair: Yes, we integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM — you supply key IDs and we use envelope encryption. For Hosted we use a managed KMS but can integrate cross-account and bring-your-own-key.
[10:17] Mark Reed: Also, for compliance we provide a runbook and SOC2 artifacts. Priya will attach those.
[10:23] Jake Morris: Appreciate that. One more thing on the demo: can you show us the route-level cost waterfall?
[10:28] Priya Nair: Yup. (opens cost panel) Waterfall starts with raw model token cost, then subtracts batching savings, prefix/KV cache delta, then adds infra overhead and reserved capacity amortization (for Dedicated). The final line is 'billed cost' which maps to your invoice or internal chargeback.
[10:46] Lina Gomez: Do you show amortized GPU-hours for dedicated as a separate column?
[10:51] Priya Nair: Yes — for Dedicated we surface GPU-hour amortization and utilization heatmap.
[10:57] Sasha Patel: Let's talk about routing policies by region. We have latency-sensitive EU users but want to avoid cross-region replication of data.
[11:05] Priya Nair: The console's routing rules let you route by geo, customer tier, or latency tail. You can also create region-specific model pins so EU traffic stays on EU-hosted models and data never leaves the region.
[11:18] Jake Morris: If we want to pilot, how fast can we get a sandbox with two routes and sample traffic?
[11:24] Mark Reed: We can spin a sandbox within 48 hours for Hosted with a sample workload. For a Private sandbox with VPC peering and KMS integration it's typically 2–3 weeks for full config.
[11:35] Lina Gomez: For the Hosted sandbox do you provide synthetic traffic generators or do we need to provide traces?
[11:41] Priya Nair: We have a built-in traffic generator and you can also upload traces for more accurate sims. For the pilot we recommend uploading a sample of your production logs.
[11:51] Sasha Patel: Regarding cost, can you show example committed capacity tiers and how they change unit economics?
[11:56] Mark Reed: (opens pricing overlay) Committed tiers vary by GPU family and monthly commitment. The console has a 'committed vs on-demand' slider in the finance tab that projects savings at different utilization.
[12:07] Jake Morris: Ok good. Do you have any built-in support for FinOps teams to map spend to chargeback codes?
[12:13] Priya Nair: Yep, cost reports include sponsor code mapping and you can export to CSV or push to your FinOps warehouse via S3.
[12:20] Lina Gomez: We're also concerned about peak-day spikes. How does Redwood handle burst capacity?
[12:26] Priya Nair: For Dedicated customers you can enable burst capacity which uses a shared pool for transient spikes. The console shows burst usage and billing separately so you can budget.
[12:36] Sasha Patel: Any mitigations to prevent a single user from triggering expensive model calls and skewing cost?
[12:42] Priya Nair: You can set per-API-key throttles and quotas as well as per-route cost limits. We also expose request tagging so anomalous spikes can be traced back to users.
[12:53] Jake Morris: Let's switch gears — can you show a recent case where batching and caching saved significant cost for a customer?
[12:58] Priya Nair: Sure, I pulled a case study. (pulls up) Company 'Meridian' reduced per-request cost by 48% by enabling prefix caching and tightening batching policies across their 3 high-volume routes. The console shows before/after: raw token cost down ~35%, effective billed cost down 48% because they also moved to committed capacity.
[13:20] Lina Gomez: That's compelling. Do you have a rough TCO model we can run with our numbers?
[13:25] Mark Reed: We'll include a TCO spreadsheet in the follow up. Priya will pre-fill it with the baseline metrics you shared.
[13:32] Sasha Patel: On integrations: we use Datadog and BigQuery. Can the console send metrics to those?
[13:38] Priya Nair: Yes. We have exporters for Datadog, Prometheus, and direct sinks to BigQuery or S3.
[13:45] Jake Morris: Anything else on security we should be aware of? Pen tests?
[13:49] Priya Nair: We do annual pen tests and can share summaries. For enterprise deals we can provide higher-fidelity test artifacts under an NDA.
[13:58] Mark Reed: Okay, we're about halfway — any customer questions before we go deeper into the route lens?
[14:04] Lina Gomez: Yeah, one more: what does the console show for cold-start costs for large models?
[14:10] Priya Nair: We show cold-start incidence and estimated warmup GPU time; for very large models we recommend reserve warm pools or smaller warm-weights to amortize. The console's util heatmap highlights cold-start spikes.
[14:23] Jake Morris: Do you expose per-request warm/cold metadata so we can filter only warm calls?
[14:29] Priya Nair: Yes, you can filter traces by cache/warm status.
[14:33] Sasha Patel: Let's look at the route-lens — you mentioned fingerprinting and tag mapping earlier.
[14:38] Priya Nair: Right. The route-lens is a composable view: top shows traffic shape, middle shows cost waterfall, bottom shows request buckets (fingerprints). You can click into a fingerprint to see example anonymized prompts and the average tokens generated.
[14:52] Lina Gomez: Fingerprinting sounds useful. Are fingerprints stable over time?
[14:57] Priya Nair: They are heuristically stable; we use a normalized template to group similar prompts. They can drift if your templates change, so we recommend periodic re-ingestion of sample traces.
[15:08] Mark Reed: Quick call-out: some transcription may show the term "KV cash" — that's me mis-speaking — it's KV cache.
[15:14] Lina Gomez: (laughs) noted.
[15:18] Jake Morris: Good to know. Any concerns about latency introduced by fingerprinting logic?
[15:24] Priya Nair: Fingerprinting is done in the telemetry pipeline asynchronously so it doesn't affect request latency.
[15:30] Sasha Patel: If we run the pilot, we'll want a dedicated review after week one to see real numbers.
[15:36] Mark Reed: Absolutely, the plan would be: day 0 spin sandbox; week 1 baseline capture; week 2 run Optimize sims and apply canary; week 3 evaluate. We'll coordinate.
[15:47] Lina Gomez: That sounds good. On logging and PII: how do you handle redaction?
[15:52] Priya Nair: By default we redact PII. You can configure additional scrubbers and also choose to disable content retention in Private deployments.
[15:59] Jake Morris: Let's talk about SLAs — for Dedicated what's typical?
[16:04] Mark Reed: Dedicated customers can get SLA-backed uptime and latency tiers; exact numbers depend on commit level. We'll share the SLA doc with the team.
[16:12] Sasha Patel: One last product question: can we run canary evals gated on business metrics (not just technical) — e.g., conversion lift?
[16:20] Priya Nair: You can push business-level labels into the trace so your downstream analytics can correlate conversions to route variants; the console can surface custom metrics if you send them back into Redwood via the metrics API.
[16:33] Jake Morris: Okay, let's capture next steps and owners.
[16:37] Mark Reed: We had agreed: we'll send the recording and deck (Mark), Priya shares SOC2 and KMS integration docs and the TCO template and a pre-filled baseline (Priya), Lina will share infra diagram and QPS expectations (Lina), and Catalyst will decide pilot start dates.
[16:52] Lina Gomez: We'll try to get those by next week.
[16:55] Jake Morris: One operational question — how hard is it to instrument our services to send the Redwood route header?
[17:02] Priya Nair: It's a small change. We support language SDKs and an HTTP header mapping. Most customers get this in under a day for two routes; we can give a sample snippet during onboarding.
[17:14] Sasha Patel: Can Redwood's SDK auto-map request metadata from our frameworks? We use FastAPI + gRPC.
[17:20] Priya Nair: We have auto-instrumentation for common frameworks and a gRPC interceptor you can drop in. We'll provide a quickstart repo.
[17:29] Jake Morris: All right. Anything else on cost?
[17:33] Mark Reed: Just that we'll include committed capacity vs on-demand projections and show the break-even point for different utilization curves in the TCO.
[17:42] Lina Gomez: That will be helpful for procurement.
[17:45] Jake Morris: For procurement, if we move to Dedicated we will need a price ceiling and a clear migration plan. Can you sketch that?
[17:52] Mark Reed: Yes — typical plan is: proof-of-value on Hosted -> purchase Dedicated reserved pool (1–3 months) -> transition routes and data plane to Dedicated -> cutover validation. We'll supply an SOW draft.
[18:06] Sasha Patel: If something goes sideways during the migration, what's the rollback path?
[18:10] Priya Nair: We keep Hosted as a fallback and use traffic mirroring. The console shows mirrored traffic differences to validate parity before cutover.
[18:20] Jake Morris: All right folks, thanks for a thorough demo. Any final Qs?
[18:25] Lina Gomez: Can you also include an example of the CSV export mapping to our GL codes? Our finance team will ask for that.
[18:31] Mark Reed: We'll include a sample CSV and mapping template.
[18:34] Priya Nair: I'll attach the security pack as well.
[18:37] Jake Morris: Great. Let's book the pilot kickoff for the week of Jan 5 — we'll confirm internally and get back to you.
[18:44] Mark Reed: Sounds good. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with all artifacts and a proposed SOW.
[18:49] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words corrected inline, some product names abbreviated. The record contains real-time demo navigation, so timestamps approximate screen changes and Q&A.

End of transcript.
